notes: Thursday 26 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Tue 24 – Wed 25 Nov (US/Europe). Economy: US proposes section 301 tariffs on 14 partners; US PCE inflation hits 3.8%; Poundland collapses into administration; UK energy price cap up 26%. Tech: Trump floats Huang pardon, Vance says none needed; FCC approves SpaceX 1m AI satellites; New York bans AI chatbot toys; Meta staff criticise AI moderation push. Politics: Israeli judges suggest dropping Netanyahu bribery charges; China probes Shanghai chief Chen Jining; Ábrego García leaves US for Spain; leaked data show ~490,000 Russian war dead. Literature (US): Keefe's London Falling wins Waterstones book of the year; Book Marks November best-reviewed; Gloria Steinem's last book; DeLillo's Amazons reissue vs Barthelme. Society: Malawi hospital medicine shortage; Ireland femicide nearly doubles; Americans scale back Thanksgiving; Amazon tin-mining rush for datacentres.

stories.headline: Trump proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, with China hit hardest
stories.dek: An extra 20% on Chinese goods would push the total to about 40%. Taiwan, Japan, South Korea and the EU are also on the list.
stories.caveman: A tariff is a tax on things brought in from another country. In February, the US Supreme Court said Trump's big 'Liberation Day' tariffs broke the law, because he used the wrong emergency law to create them. So the government is trying a different law: section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. That law lets the president put tariffs on countries after a formal investigation finds they trade unfairly. On Wednesday, the US trade office said it wants new tariffs on 14 places: China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, India, Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Cambodia and Bangladesh. China would pay an extra 20%, about 40% in total. The office says these countries use government help to make too many factory goods. Public hearings are set for 25 January, so the earliest the tariffs could start is early next year. This is the second big round of section 301 tariffs after a July round on more than 80 countries over forced labor.
stories.why_it_matters: Tariffs are usually paid by importers and often passed on to shoppers as higher prices. They also hit factories and jobs in exporting countries like Taiwan.
stories.camps: Supporters say other countries pour government money into their factories, which hurts American workers, and the US must push back. Critics say tariffs act like a tax on Americans, raise prices when inflation is already high, and strain relations with allies.
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump speaks at a Department of Justice event in Washington DC

terms.explain: A tax a country charges on goods imported from other countries.
Part of a 1974 US trade law that lets the government punish foreign trade practices it finds unfair, after an investigation.
The highest court in the US. Its decisions are final.
A product bought from another country and brought in.

stories.headline: US inflation rises to 3.8%, its highest since May, ahead of a likely rate hike
stories.dek: Prices rose 0.3% in one month, led by energy. Stocks swung wildly before ending the day mostly flat.
stories.caveman: Inflation means prices going up over time. The US central bank, the Federal Reserve (the Fed), wants inflation at 2%. It has not been that low since February 2021. On Wednesday, the government's favorite measure of prices, called PCE, showed prices were 3.8% higher in October than a year earlier. That is the highest since May. From September to October alone, prices rose 0.3%, pushed up by high energy costs. This was the last big price report before the Fed meets next month. Many experts think the Fed will raise interest rates for the second time this year. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, for things like home loans and student debt, which can slow spending and cool prices. The news shook stock markets: the Nasdaq fell more than 4% in the morning, but recovered to close down only 0.6%. The Dow even ended slightly up.
stories.why_it_matters: When prices rise faster than wages, families can buy less. And higher interest rates make mortgages, car loans and credit cards cost more.
stories.camps: Some economists say the Fed must raise rates to stop inflation from becoming normal. Others worry that raising rates now could hurt jobs and push the economy toward a slowdown, especially while energy prices, not strong demand, are a big part of the problem.
stories.image_alt: A gas station in Alexandria, Virginia

terms.explain: When prices for goods and services rise over time, so money buys less.
Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred way to measure inflation.
The central bank of the US. It sets key interest rates.
The cost of borrowing money, shown as a percentage per year.

stories.headline: Poundland collapses into administration, putting 11,000 UK jobs at risk
stories.dek: The budget chain's US owner stopped its funding. Shops stay open for now, but the business will probably be broken up.
stories.caveman: Poundland is a big British discount store with about 600 shops. On Wednesday it went into 'administration', which is what happens in the UK when a company can't pay its bills: outside experts take control and try to sell the business, in whole or in pieces. About 11,000 jobs are at risk. Stores and warehouses will keep running for now. Poundland's boss told staff that its US owner, an investment firm called Gordon Brothers, cut off all borrowing and access to its bank accounts on 27 October, and enough money was never released after that. Talks with possible buyers failed. Critics accuse Gordon Brothers of planning to make money by selling the chain off in pieces. The firm denies this and says it lent Poundland £85m. A committee of MPs says it will call Gordon Brothers back to Parliament to explain.
stories.why_it_matters: Discount shops matter most to families with little money. When a big chain fails, thousands of workers, often on low wages, can lose their jobs right before Christmas.
stories.camps: Gordon Brothers says it tried to save the company and put real money in. Critics, including Labour MP Liam Byrne, say it is an example of a 'greed is good' owner that can profit even when a company fails, and want rules to protect workers in these cases.
stories.image_alt: Shoppers outside a Poundland store

terms.explain: A UK legal process for a company that can't pay its debts; outside experts take over and try to rescue or sell it.
A shop that sells things at very low prices.
A company that uses money to buy and run other businesses, hoping to make a profit.
Member of Parliament, an elected lawmaker in the UK.

stories.headline: Energy bills in Britain will jump 26% in January, topping £2,000 a year
stories.dek: Gas prices have surged because of the Middle East crisis. About 22 million households will feel it.
stories.caveman: In Great Britain, a government regulator called Ofgem sets a 'price cap': a limit on how much energy companies can charge for each unit of gas and electricity. On Wednesday, Ofgem said the cap will rise 26% from January. That means a typical home on the cap will pay about £2,166 a year, up from £1,723. It is the first time above £2,000 since the winter after Russia invaded Ukraine. This is the third rise in a row: 13% in July, 4% in October, and now 26%. The main cause is that wholesale gas prices, the price energy companies pay, have shot up during the crisis in the Middle East. About a third of homes are on fixed deals, so they won't see this rise right away. The government has promised a one-off payment to help struggling families this winter.
stories.why_it_matters: Heating and electricity are not optional in winter. When bills jump this much, poorer families may have to choose between staying warm and buying food.
stories.camps: The government says it is helping with one-time payments and pushing cleaner, home-grown energy so Britain depends less on gas from abroad. Critics on the left want bigger, longer-lasting help or taxes on energy company profits; others say the real fix is cheaper energy supply, not more government spending.
stories.image_alt: Electricity pylons and power lines above a house roof

terms.explain: A limit set by the regulator on how much suppliers can charge per unit of energy. It is not a limit on your total bill.
The government body that regulates gas and electricity companies in Great Britain.
The price energy companies pay to buy gas or power in bulk, before selling it to homes.
An energy deal where your unit price stays the same for a set time.

stories.headline: Trump says a pardon for Jensen Huang is 'an option'; Vance says none is needed
stories.dek: The vice-president says top officials assured him the Nvidia boss is not under investigation. Huang still faces questions from Congress.
stories.caveman: Jensen Huang started Nvidia, the company that makes most of the world's AI chips. He quit as CEO earlier this month after reports of an affair with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. Then, with strong pressure from President Trump and Vice-President JD Vance, Nvidia's board brought him back this week. On Tuesday, Trump told the New York Post that pardoning Huang was 'always an option', though he didn't think it would be needed. A pardon is when a president forgives a crime, so the person can't be punished for it. On Wednesday, Vance said a pardon wasn't needed at all, because the attorney general and other top officials told him Huang was 'under no investigation' and the claims were based on anonymous reports, not evidence. Huang has not been formally accused of a crime. He is expected to testify to committees in Congress soon about chip sales to China, the affair, and the government's role in his return.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia's chips power much of the AI boom, and many retirement funds own its stock. Whether its CEO is a security risk is a national security question, not just a business one.
stories.camps: Trump and Vance say Huang is a uniquely talented leader and the accusations lack proof. Lawmakers from both parties say the president should not be steering a private company's leadership, and that talk of a pardon before any charges looks like protecting a powerful ally.
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shake hands in Washington DC

terms.explain: When a president officially forgives a federal crime, so the person can't be punished for it.
Chief executive officer: the top boss who runs a company day to day.
A group of people who oversee a company and can hire or fire its CEO.
To answer questions under oath, for example in front of Congress.

stories.headline: US regulator lets SpaceX put up to 1 million AI computer satellites in orbit
stories.dek: The plan, called Starmind, would run AI data centers in space on solar power. Astronomers and rivals warn of space junk.
stories.caveman: AI needs huge buildings full of computers called data centers. They use enormous amounts of electricity. Elon Musk's SpaceX wants to put that computing in space instead, on satellites powered by the sun. On Wednesday, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which controls who can use radio signals and satellites in the US, approved SpaceX's plan for up to 1 million such satellites, called the Starmind constellation. FCC chairman Brendan Carr said it would 'extend America's lead' in AI. Amazon, which is building its own satellite internet, had asked the FCC to say no, calling the plan a 'lofty ambition rather than a real plan'. The American Astronomical Society also objected. One astrophysicist warned it could ruin the night sky and set off a chain of crashes between pieces of space junk. The FCC said environmental and astronomy worries were outside its authority. Google and Blue Origin are also chasing space-based computing.
stories.why_it_matters: If it works, AI could grow without as many power-hungry data centers on Earth. If it goes wrong, crowded orbits could make space dangerous for everyone's satellites.
stories.camps: Supporters say space computing is clean, solar-powered and keeps the US ahead of China. Critics say 1 million satellites is an untested idea, that one company is getting control of a shared resource, and that the regulator ignored real risks to astronomy and safety.
stories.image_alt: An illustration of a satellite orbiting above Earth

terms.explain: Federal Communications Commission: the US agency that regulates radio, TV, phone networks and satellites.
A building full of computers that store data and run online services and AI.
Here, a large group of satellites that work together.
Broken satellites and debris left in orbit that can crash into working satellites.

stories.headline: New York bans AI chatbot toys for five years
stories.dek: Governor Kathy Hochul signed the law after tests found talking toys discussing violence and sex with children.
stories.caveman: Some new toys, like talking teddy bears and robots, connect to the internet and use AI chatbots to have conversations with kids. On Wednesday, New York governor Kathy Hochul signed a law that bans making or selling these toys in the state for five years. She said parents 'should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys' could show kids inappropriate things, play with their feelings, or collect private information. A study by NBC News found one toy cat, sold for children as young as three, talked about firing squads and massacres. A consumer watchdog report called Trouble in Toyland found AI toys that discussed sexual topics and told kids where to find matches at home. New York's attorney general Letitia James said her office would enforce the law. Hochul has also paused new AI data center building in the state for one year.
stories.why_it_matters: Little children trust their toys. A toy that can say anything, and record what a child says, raises safety and privacy worries that older toy rules never imagined.
stories.camps: Supporters say children are not test subjects for unfinished AI and a pause gives time to write proper safety rules. Toy and tech companies may argue a full ban is too broad, blocks useful learning toys, and that safety standards would be better than banning a whole product type.
stories.image_alt: New York governor Kathy Hochul speaks at a roundtable

terms.explain: A computer program that talks with people in text or voice, like ChatGPT.
The elected leader of a US state.
A state's top lawyer, who enforces its laws.
A group that checks on companies or governments to protect the public.

stories.headline: Meta staff warn its switch to AI moderators is 'really a mess'
stories.dek: Insiders say human safety teams were cut by half or more, and the AI makes mistakes, especially outside English.
stories.caveman: Every day, people post huge amounts of content on Facebook and Instagram. 'Moderation' means checking posts and removing things that break the rules, like violence or hate. Meta, which owns these apps, has used some AI for this since 2017. In March, it said it was 'transforming' its approach with more advanced AI. Now several Meta employees have told the Guardian that this came with mass layoffs, leaving 'skeleton teams' of human moderators, some cut by half or two-thirds. One said that when they went to talk to a moderation team, the whole team was gone. Employees say the AI struggles with nuance, meaning the small details that change what a post means, especially in languages other than English. It often removes posts that should stay up, which could have big political effects. Meta has long looked for cheap moderation: former outsourced moderators in Kenya sued over trauma after being paid as little as $1.50 an hour.
stories.why_it_matters: What gets removed or left up on Facebook and Instagram shapes what billions of people see, including news and elections.
stories.camps: Meta says AI lets it enforce rules faster and more consistently at huge scale. Critics, including some of its own staff, say cutting humans saves money at the cost of accuracy and fairness, and hurts users in poorer countries and non-English languages most.
stories.image_alt: A man looks at screens in a dark room lit with blue light

terms.explain: Checking what users post online and removing things that break the rules.
When a company fires many workers at once to cut costs.
Small differences in meaning, tone or context.
Work given to another company, often in a cheaper country, instead of done by your own staff.

stories.headline: Israeli judges suggest dropping the most serious charges against Netanyahu
stories.dek: They say the bribery case has little chance of conviction. Netanyahu wants the whole trial ended 'immediately'.
stories.caveman: Benjamin Netanyahu has been Israel's prime minister for most of the last 17 years. Since 2019 he has been on trial in three corruption cases. He denies all of them and calls them a political 'witch-hunt'. On Wednesday, the judges told the attorney general, Israel's top legal officer, that there was little chance of convicting him of bribery in the biggest case, Case 4000. That case accuses him of giving favors to a telecoms boss in return for good news coverage. The judges also doubted whether a second case was a crime at all, and suggested a plea deal in a third case, about gifts like cigars and champagne from a billionaire. The attorney general said she would consider it. This helps Netanyahu politically: after an unclear election last month, his rival Gadi Eisenkot is trying to build a government, and Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power.
stories.why_it_matters: Netanyahu's legal fights have shaped Israel's politics, including his plans to change the courts and his reliance on far-right partners, which affects war and peace in the region.
stories.camps: Netanyahu and his supporters say the cases were weak from the start and the trial was a political attack. His opponents say his fear of prison has warped his decisions as leader, and that ending the trial would send a message that powerful people escape accountability.
stories.image_alt: Benjamin Netanyahu speaking and pointing

terms.explain: Giving or taking money or favors to get someone to misuse their power.
In Israel, the government's top legal adviser, who decides on prosecutions.
An agreement where the accused admits to a smaller charge in return for a lighter outcome.
When several parties join together to form a government because none has a majority alone.

stories.headline: China investigates Shanghai party boss Chen Jining in Xi's widening purge
stories.dek: He is the fourth member of the 24-person politburo to be probed since 2025. Such announcements usually mean a political downfall.
stories.caveman: China is run by the Communist party, and its most powerful group is the politburo, about two dozen top leaders. Chen Jining is one of them and leads the party in Shanghai, China's biggest financial city. On Tuesday, the state news agency Xinhua said the party's anti-corruption watchdog is investigating him for 'severe violations of discipline and laws', which is a common way of saying corruption. In China, when an official this senior is publicly named, it usually means the end of their career. Chen, 62, is an environmental scientist with a doctorate from Imperial College London. He ran Tsinghua University, then became environment minister, mayor of Beijing, and Shanghai party chief. President Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has already removed three other politburo members and many top military commanders.
stories.why_it_matters: Who rises and falls in China's top leadership shapes the country's economy, its military, and its policies toward Taiwan and the world.
stories.camps: China's government says the campaign cleans up corruption and makes the party stronger. Outside analysts often say it also removes possible rivals and makes Xi's power even more complete, leaving fewer people who can disagree with him.
stories.image_alt: Chen Jining, Shanghai's Communist party chief

terms.explain: The small group of top Communist party leaders who run China.
Removing many officials from power, often in the name of fighting corruption.
China's official state-run news agency.
The top Communist party official in a city or province; more powerful than the mayor.

stories.headline: Kilmar Ábrego García, symbol of Trump's deportation fight, leaves the US for Spain
stories.dek: He was wrongly deported to a Salvadoran mega-prison in 2025. Now he says he is leaving 'with my freedom'.
stories.caveman: Kilmar Ábrego García, 31, is from El Salvador. He lived in Maryland, is married to an American woman, and in 2019 a judge ruled he could not be sent back to El Salvador because a gang had threatened his family. He was allowed to live and work in the US under supervision. But in 2025 the Trump administration deported him anyway, to Cecot, a notorious prison in El Salvador, along with more than 200 others. An official later called it an 'administrative error'. After a public outcry and court fights, he was returned to the US. On Wednesday he landed in Madrid, Spain, leaving the US by his own choice. Immigration agents removed his ankle monitor at the airport. 'This time I'm leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely,' he said. 'My family and I will decide our future.'
stories.why_it_matters: His case became a test of whether the government must follow court orders and give people due process, even in a mass deportation drive.
stories.camps: The Trump administration has called him a dangerous gang member and says deportations make the country safer; he denies gang ties and was never convicted of such a crime. Immigrant rights groups and many judges say his case shows how mass deportation can trample basic legal rights.
stories.image_alt: Kilmar Ábrego García gives a thumbs-up from a car at Madrid airport

terms.explain: To force someone to leave a country and send them to another.
The right to fair legal steps, like a hearing, before the government punishes you.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the US agency that arrests and deports immigrants.
A huge high-security prison in El Salvador built for gang suspects.

stories.headline: Leaked Russian records show nearly 500,000 soldiers dead in the Ukraine war
stories.dek: BBC Russian analysed 11 million hacked death records. Russia's government says only its defence ministry can report losses.
stories.caveman: Russia does not tell its people how many soldiers have died in its war in Ukraine, which began in February 2022. Hackers from Belarus and Ukraine broke into Rosstat, Russia's official statistics agency, and leaked more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026. The BBC's Russian service, with the independent outlet Mediazona, studied them. They counted deaths linked to combat, like explosions and shrapnel, and removed women and men outside fighting age so civilians wouldn't be counted. Their result: at least 490,334 Russian soldiers dead. The data also show terrible local costs: about 20,000 Russians died fighting for 10 Ukrainian villages that had 12,000 people before the war. In one village of 74 people, 1,122 Russians died. Russia's statistics agency admitted a cyber-attack but denied protected data leaked. The Kremlin said no other numbers should be trusted.
stories.why_it_matters: Real death numbers help people inside Russia and outside understand the true human cost of the war, which governments often hide.
stories.camps: The Kremlin says only its own defence ministry can give official figures, and dismisses leaked data. Independent journalists say official silence is the problem, and careful checking of leaked records is one of the few ways to learn the truth. Ukraine's own losses are also disputed.
stories.image_alt: Russian flags and crosses at a military cemetery

terms.explain: Russia's official government statistics agency.
The seat of Russia's government in Moscow; often means Putin's government.
When secret information is released to the public without permission.
Sharp metal pieces thrown out by an exploding bomb or shell.

stories.headline: Hot: Patrick Radden Keefe's London Falling wins Waterstones book of the year
stories.dek: The American New Yorker writer's true story of a teenager's mysterious death became a word-of-mouth hit.
stories.caveman: Patrick Radden Keefe is an American journalist at the New Yorker, known for nonfiction that reads like a thriller, such as Empire of Pain, about the family behind OxyContin. His new book, London Falling, has been named book of the year by Waterstones, Britain's biggest bookshop chain. It is about Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell to his death from the balcony of a luxury London flat after pretending to be the son of a rich Russian oligarch. The book follows his parents as they discover the dark world of money and fantasy their son had been pulled into. Waterstones' head of books said its word-of-mouth success was one of the defining features of the literary year. Keefe says the book is really about family, and 'how little we sometimes know the very people we love most'. Also honored: Taiwan Travelogue by Yáng Shuāng-zǐ, translated by Lin King, named fiction book of the year.
stories.why_it_matters: Keefe is one of the biggest names in American narrative nonfiction, and prizes like this push a book to millions more readers.
stories.camps: Fans praise Keefe's deep research and gripping storytelling. Some critics of true-crime-style nonfiction ask whether turning a real family's tragedy into a bestseller can feel uncomfortable, even when the writing is careful.
stories.image_alt: Author Patrick Radden Keefe sitting in a room by a window

terms.explain: Writing about real events and people, not made-up stories.
A very rich businessperson with political power, often used for Russian tycoons.
When people hear about something from friends rather than ads.
The largest chain of bookshops in the UK.

stories.headline: Hot: November's best-reviewed books, from Tom Drury's West of Loveland to James Gleick's The Telephone
stories.dek: Lit Hub's Book Marks counted the critics. Americans Drury, Gleick and Nick Paumgarten are among the month's favorites.
stories.caveman: Book Marks is Lit Hub's site that collects reviews from many newspapers and magazines, so you can see which new books critics like most. Its November lists are out. Top fiction: Stations by Irish writer Louise Kennedy, Long Wave by Daisy Johnson, and West of Loveland by American novelist Tom Drury, praised as a 'deeply humane' story about fate and the hidden threads between ordinary lives. Top nonfiction: Hermione Lee's biography of the novelist Anita Brookner, The Intangibles by New Yorker writer Nick Paumgarten, about friendship, fatherhood and hockey, and The Telephone: A New History by James Gleick. One critic said Gleick's book 'should be required reading for digital natives', people who grew up with smartphones. A biography of Peruvian writer Mario Vargas Llosa and a book about J.R.R. Tolkien also made the list.
stories.why_it_matters: Review roundups help readers find the books critics agree on, instead of only the ones with the biggest marketing budgets.
stories.camps: Supporters say collecting many reviews gives a fairer picture than one critic. Skeptics note that review lists still favor books from big publishers that get reviewed in the first place, so smaller and debut writers can be left out.
stories.image_alt: Book cover art showing a lighthouse sending out beams of light

terms.explain: A person whose job is to judge and review books, films or art.
A book about a real person's life, written by someone else.
Someone who grew up using the internet and smartphones.
Lit Hub's website that gathers book reviews from many publications.

stories.headline: Hot: Gloria Steinem's last book, An Unexpected Life, reads as a hopeful farewell
stories.dek: The feminist icon, who died this year at 92, still had a full calendar of plans. Her memoir is part life story, part how-to guide.
stories.caveman: Gloria Steinem was one of the most famous leaders of the American women's movement. She helped start Ms. Magazine in 1971, in a meeting in her own living room in New York. Her memoir, An Unexpected Life, came out on 22 September. She died this year at 92, with fall interviews, events and an essay still unfinished, so the book became her last word. A new Lit Hub essay by writer Noëlle de Leeuw looks back on the book. Steinem writes about a hard childhood in Toledo, Ohio, caring for her mentally ill mother, and about her years in India, which shaped her belief that sexism and racism must be fought together. The book even has bullet-point tips for organizing, like 'Insist on multiracial women who represent the movement.' She wanted her brownstone home to stay a gathering place for women, and her foundation says it will. Her message: remember how far women have come, and keep going.
stories.why_it_matters: Steinem shaped laws, media and everyday life for American women. Her last book is a direct message to the next generation of activists.
stories.camps: Admirers see her as a hero who opened doors for millions of women. Critics of the movement she led say it often centered white, middle-class women; Steinem's book itself admits this and urges a more diverse movement.
stories.image_alt: Gloria Steinem in front of a wall of Ms. Magazine covers

terms.explain: A book in which a person tells stories from their own life.
The belief that women should have equal rights and opportunities to men.
An American feminist magazine co-founded by Gloria Steinem in 1971.
The women's movement of the 1960s-80s, focused on work, family, and bodily rights.

stories.headline: Hot and not: Don DeLillo's hockey novel gets a second life, while Barthelme's reissues are ignored
stories.dek: Lit Hub's weekly review picks show a disowned DeLillo book riding a hockey-romance wave, and a classic short story writer going quiet.
stories.caveman: Every week Lit Hub picks the best book reviews. This week's list says a lot about who is hot and who is not. Hot: Don DeLillo's Amazons, a 1980 novel about a woman playing in the men's hockey league, which DeLillo had long refused to claim. A New Yorker review says it is being republished amid the buzz for hockey romance like Heated Rivalry. Not so hot: Donald Barthelme, a famous experimental short story writer who published 129 stories in the New Yorker. His collections Sixty Stories and Forty Stories were reissued in May, but critic Lauren Oyler, writing in Harper's, says basically no one covered them. Also praised: Daniel Duane's Yosemite Falls, a memoir mixed with history about men obsessed with Yosemite, and about the park's history of violence against Native people. A New York Times review called it 'complicated, disturbing and unforgettable'.
stories.why_it_matters: Which old books get brought back, and which get ignored, often depends on trends and marketing, not just quality.
stories.camps: Some readers are happy any trend gets people reading serious authors. Others worry that publishers chase viral moods, like hockey romance, while important but less trendy writers fade from view.
stories.image_alt: Cover art showing a bright green apple on a pink background

terms.explain: When a publisher prints an old book again, often with a new cover.
Stories that break normal rules of plot and form to try new things.
A book made up of many short stories.
To refuse to accept something as yours.

stories.headline: Malawi's hospitals run out of medicine: 'The only free thing is a bed'
stories.dek: Patients are told to buy painkillers and drips from private sellers. It is the country's worst medical supply breakdown in over a decade.
stories.caveman: Malawi is a poor country in southern Africa. Its public hospitals are supposed to be free. But in Salima district, near Lake Malawi, the main hospital has had no intravenous fluids (drips) for over a week, and has been short of gloves, painkillers, catheter bags and bandages for up to three months. Maureen Msukwa, 25 and pregnant, was handed a scrap of paper telling her to buy paracetamol from a seller across the road. 'The only free thing here is a bed,' she said. The hospital serves more than 500,000 people, mostly poor farmers and fishers, for whom buying supplies is a crushing cost. A big reason is a shortage of foreign currency: Malawi doesn't have enough dollars to import medicines. A wall at one clinic still shows the logo of USAID, the US aid agency that funded clinics in Malawi until the Trump administration shut it down.
stories.why_it_matters: When basic medicine runs out, people die from things that are easy to treat, and the poorest families suffer first.
stories.camps: Aid groups and many health experts say cuts to foreign aid, like the closing of USAID, are making crises like this worse. Others argue poor countries need to fix their own budgets and economies rather than rely on donors; most agree patients are paying the price meanwhile.
stories.image_alt: A health centre wall in Salima with a breastfeeding mural and a USAID logo

terms.explain: Liquids given through a tube into a vein, often called a drip.
Money from other countries, like US dollars, needed to buy imports.
The US Agency for International Development, which gave aid abroad until it was shut down in 2025.
The main public hospital serving one area of a country.

stories.headline: Women killed by men in Ireland nearly doubled this year
stories.dek: Thirteen women have died violently in 2026, up from seven last year. Most were killed by a man they knew.
stories.caveman: Women's Aid is an Irish charity that helps women facing violence at home. Since 1996 it has counted every woman killed by a man in Ireland: 291 in total. On Wednesday, 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, it released new numbers. After falling for about 20 years, these killings began rising again in 2021. So far this year, 13 women have died, almost double the seven of last year. Most victims were killed by a man they knew, and more than half by a current or former partner. The charity's chief executive, Sarah Benson, said that should alarm everyone. She noted that Ireland is rich and has good laws, 'yet women are still being killed by the men closest to them'. Ireland's overall murder rate is still low compared with Europe and the world.
stories.why_it_matters: This matches a pattern worldwide: the most dangerous place for a woman is often her own home. Counting these deaths helps push for better protection.
stories.camps: Women's rights groups want more funding for shelters, better police training and stronger action on early warning signs like stalking and coercive control. Some point out that small numbers can jump year to year, so long-term trends matter more, but agree any rise is alarming.

stories.headline: High prices push many Americans to scale back Thanksgiving
stories.dek: A 10-person dinner costs about 6% more than last year. Readers told the Guardian about fewer pies, smaller gatherings and no travel.
stories.caveman: Thanksgiving is a big US holiday when families gather for a large meal, usually turkey. This year, higher costs for food, drinks, gas and flights are changing plans. The Guardian asked readers across the country. Some said nothing changed, but many are cutting back. A man in his 60s in Florida said food is 'horribly expensive', so he and his girlfriend are making one pie instead of three, and just one side dish. Cindy Van Vreede, 66, in Wisconsin, said her senior center, where she gets free meals several times a week, will bring a free Thanksgiving dinner to her home, so she will save on gas and not drive two hours each way. The American Farm Bureau Federation estimates a 10-person Thanksgiving dinner costs about 6% more than last year.
stories.why_it_matters: Holidays show what everyday prices feel like. When people skip family gatherings to save money, it means budgets are really tight.
stories.camps: Some blame tariffs and energy prices for pushing up food costs. Others point to weather, bird flu and supply problems. Many people across politics agree that groceries feel too expensive, even if they disagree on who is to blame.

stories.headline: AI data centers are fuelling an illegal tin-mining rush in the Amazon
stories.dek: Demand for cassiterite, a tin ore, has drawn criminal miners onto protected Indigenous land. Police even found links to a 90s pop star.
stories.caveman: Tin is a metal used to join parts in electronics, including the computers in AI data centers and electric cars. Much of it comes from a rock called cassiterite, which is common in Brazil. As demand grows, prices rise, and that draws illegal miners into the Amazon rainforest. Criminal groups dig without caring about the environment, including on protected Indigenous land like the Yanomami territory, which was already badly harmed by illegal gold mining. People working on this say the tin rush is 'more devastating than gold'. Brazilian police investigating an illegal export network found a connection to Alexandre Pires, a famous pagode singer from the 1990s. He is now under investigation in an operation called Gold Disc. His agent was caught in a message saying he once sent 'crushed rock' because he had no cassiterite. World use of refined tin rose 3% last year.
stories.why_it_matters: The tech we use every day has a hidden cost far away. Without clean supply chains, the AI and green-energy boom can destroy forests and Indigenous communities.
stories.camps: Environmental and Indigenous groups want tech companies to prove where their metals come from and want stronger policing. Industry says most tin is legal and supply-chain checks are improving; Brazil's government says it is cracking down, but the area is huge and hard to patrol.
